p40: On R&D, we continued to invest at full strength because model leadership is the prerequisite for everything else. In the first half of 2026, the company’s R&D expenditure reached RMB 2.13 billion, equivalent to approximately US$317 million. Loss for the period was approximately RMB 2.072 billion, down 12.1% year on year. The loss ratio narrowed by a factor of 4.7 compared with the first half of last year. Adjusted net loss was RMB 1.964 billion, and the adjusted loss ratio narrowed by a factor of 3.5 compared with the first half of last year. It is clear that, while revenue is scaling up, unit economics are also improving rapidly.
p41: It is particularly noteworthy that adjusted net loss in the first half of this year was RMB 1.964 billion, lower than R&D expenditure. This indicates that, following the pattern seen in last year’s annual results, gross profit generated by the business：after initially covering administrative and selling expenses：has begun to support R&D investment.
p42: Next is the third section. I will discuss the company’s operating performance behind the financial figures from five perspectives.
p43: First, the revenue mix has undergone a fundamental change. In the first half of 2026, the open-platform and API business accounted for 86.5% of revenue. This was not the result of deliberate financial engineering; it was the natural evolution brought about by improvements in model capability. Looking back at the company’s business development, we moved from selling locally deployed models two years ago, to API usage and subscription plans, and now to selling end-to-end task outcomes. As model intelligence improved, new scenarios and business formats were unlocked one after another.
p44: As models become capable of independently completing increasingly complete tasks, what customers purchase increasingly resembles the result itself, and the unit in which revenue is measured changes accordingly. Before 2025, in the first stage, the company primarily developed locally deployed-model business. At that time, early models were not yet capable of independently completing a full job. Users were buying a tool, and that tool needed to be integrated, customized, and delivered into the customer’s own environment. It also needed to meet requirements for data security, compliance, and autonomy and controllability. Local deployment was therefore the natural starting point for enterprise adoption of large models at that time.
p45: From the beginning of 2025, the company gradually entered the second stage: the Coding stage. The defining characteristic of this stage was the model’s transition from knowledge-driven behavior to task-driven behavior. Improvements in programming capability drove rapid growth in APIs and subscription products such as CodingPlan.
p46: At this stage, the company strategically scaled back software-licensing business for locally deployed models and shifted toward continuously providing intelligence services that are callable, scalable, and measurable. Since the beginning of this year, the company has entered the third stage: the Agentic and Cowork stage. The business is moving from model calls toward task delivery. In the first half of 2026, GLM models continued to improve in Agent planning, tool use, and sustained execution of long-horizon tasks. The business also expanded from single-point coding applications into high-value scenarios such as software engineering, cybersecurity, data analysis, and complex automation. The business model is progressing from selling usage volume toward selling subscriptions and end-to-end task outcomes.
p47: Looking ahead, Cowork is precisely the stage the company is now opening up. Models connect to enterprise data, tools, and business systems and are embedded in procurement, finance, customer service, R&D, IT operations, and other processes. They already possess the foundations needed to move from understanding a requirement to executing the task. Real enterprise workflows can, in turn, become environments and data from which models learn. During the first half of 2026, the company began trials in cybersecurity, legal services, finance, education, and other areas.
p48: Cybersecurity is currently progressing the fastest. The other areas remain at an early stage and have not yet generated revenue at scale. Connecting the three stages of local deployment, Coding, and Cowork, the core logic is this: each time a model makes a leap in capability and becomes able to complete a more substantial task, what customers purchase moves closer to the final economic value and outcome, and the company’s revenue structure is rewritten accordingly. This is the fundamental reason for the change in revenue mix.
p49: Second, our go-to-market strategy has broadened further. In addition to model scores on various benchmarks, the industry is paying increasing attention to whether models can achieve a Pareto-optimal combination of intelligence and cost. In the first half of 2026, the company continued to deepen its presence in high-value task scenarios while also launching GLM-5.3 Flash, with the aim of demonstrating that frontier intelligence can also enter broadly accessible use cases.
p50: Relying on clusters of more than 100,000 domestic accelerator cards, the company has initially achieved ultra-large-scale, low-cost inference. At the end of last month, the company opened CodingPlan subscriptions to all users, covering Light, Pro, Max, and team editions. This is one of the earlier large-model services in China to deliver programming-agent capabilities through a subscription model. In addition to meeting enterprise needs through APIs, we also hope to provide Chinese developers with high-quality subscription-based programming plans. From high-value tasks to the parallel pursuit of frontier intelligence and broad accessibility, and from enterprise services to a combination of APIs and CodingPlan, the company’s go-to-market strategy is becoming deeper, broader, and more balanced.
p51: Third, for the first time, we are providing a detailed discussion of the MaaS platform’s user scale, depth of use, and user quality. As of August 2026, the platform had more than 7.4 million registered users, up 144% from the beginning of the year. Paying daily active users increased by 603%. From a revenue perspective, the top ten users’ average daily usage this month was 98 times the level at the beginning of the year. These data points, taken together, show that we have built one of China’s largest independent developer platforms, and that the total user base continues to grow rapidly from an already substantial base. Over the past two months, driven by GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.3 Flash, the number of users rose by 1.6 million：from 5.8 million at the end of June to 7.4 million.
p52: This shows that, after entering the era of long-horizon tasks, heavy developer users are generating average daily platform usage far beyond that of the earlier vibe-coding stage, both in scale and in depth of use within real workflows. At the same time, the platform’s high-quality user base continues to expand. As of the end of August, on an ARR basis, the numbers of high-quality user cohorts contributing more than US$100,000, US$500,000, US$1 million, US$10 million, US$25 million, and US$250 million on an annualized basis were, respectively, 115, 25, 37, 8, 2, and 2. Those are the figures for user scale, user profile, depth of use, and user quality.
p53: Fourth, we are introducing a new concept: the compute multiplier. This concept has received broad attention in the industry in recent years. It reflects the open-platform and API revenue generated for every RMB 1 invested in compute, with compute investment including both training and inference. The company’s compute multiplier this year increased fourteenfold compared with the first half of last year, demonstrating a significant improvement in the efficiency of compute supply.
p54: The improvement in this curve comes from two directions. First, the intelligence carried by each token continues to increase, while token consumption and cost per task continue to decline. Second, the revenue generated by each RMB 1 of compute investment continues to increase, meaning the model’s ability to fund its own development is steadily strengthening. Breakthroughs in intelligence bring greater token usage and commercial returns; those returns are then reinvested in compute and R&D, further raising the intelligence frontier. This flywheel has begun to turn.
p55: Fifth, safety capabilities are growing in step with model capabilities. For model capability to become a dependable service, the key question is whether it can earn trust in the real world. We have always adhered to the simultaneous development of openness and safety. On the one hand, through open model weights, the MaaS platform, CodingPlan, and a global developer network, we enable models to enter as many real-world environments as possible. On the other hand, through permission controls, process monitoring, risk assessments, vulnerability disclosure, and external validation, we establish verifiability of the model’s capabilities.
p56: That concludes the discussion of the company’s financial performance and business development. Next, Zhipu Chairman Liu Debin will discuss the outlook.
p57: In the first half of 2026, we demonstrated that a model can independently complete a full job. The next step is to enable a model to undertake a complete business process. We have developed several judgments around this objective.
p58: First, from the perspective of model tasks, models are evolving from long-horizon tasks toward autonomous systems. The current frontier consists of engineering tasks lasting several hours. The next step will extend this to complete interactions lasting several days, enabling a model to maintain goal consistency over longer periods, continuously decompose tasks, call tools, interact with the environment, repair errors, and verify results. At the same time, the industry will move from a single Agent to multi-Agent division of labor and collaboration, with models undertaking complete business processes and moving from assisting work to executing work.
p59: The threshold for this step does not lie entirely in intelligence itself; it lies even more in reliability and auditability. Models need to work without humans checking every step, while still leaving a trail that can be reviewed.
p60: Second, from the perspective of capability evolution, scaling has never stopped and remains the primary path toward higher intelligence. What has not changed is the path; what has changed is the object being scaled. The current upper bound of a model is determined by a combination of four factors: base-model scale, effective depth, training depth, and task environment. The marginal returns of these four factors differ and rotate across stages. The company allocates resources by judging which factor offers the highest current return at each stage.
p61: GLM-5.3 demonstrates that training depth is currently the area with the greatest room for improvement. Once post-training has been pushed to its limit, the next stage of growth must return to the base model. GLM-5.3 Flash has already validated efficiency through a next-generation architecture and a 30 TG multimodal corpus. The next-generation base model is already in training, with directions including greater effective scale, longer native context, and native unified multimodal modeling.
p62: Third, we aim to achieve self-training at the system level. A deeper change is occurring inside the training system: data, environments, and infrastructure are all showing early signs of being taken over by AI.
p63: Data is beginning to generate itself. Model-versus-model self-play pipelines mean that the upper bound of data quality is no longer determined by the speed of human annotation, but by the model’s own ability to verify results.
p64: Environments are beginning to be manufactured. Research agents collect task patterns, judge agents attempt each task, and verifiers and environments are synthesized automatically, gradually becoming standardized products on the pipeline.
p65: Infrastructure is beginning to optimize itself. Inference-system optimization is fundamentally a code-engineering task, and this is precisely the capability domain in which models are strongest.
p66: These three lines point toward the same end state: models participate in their own improvement, forming recursive self-improvement. This is our technology vision：self-training. The next-generation GLM will self-train in environments built by the previous generation of GLM.
p67: Fourth, boundaries and governance. The stronger a capability becomes, the more important it is to place evaluation and judgment in external hands. Assessment of model capabilities and judgments about risk must ultimately be made by people, with independent evaluation by external organizations. In the first half of 2026, we had already begun putting this into practice in cybersecurity. The most sensitive capabilities are released under controlled conditions. Before open-sourcing, independent assessments are conducted by professional third-party teams. Vulnerabilities are responsibly disclosed through the national vulnerability database. Benchmark scores are reported by the company. Risk judgments are left to external teams. This division of labor will not change as capabilities improve; it will only become stronger as those capabilities advance.
p68: Finally, I would like to summarize all of today’s figures in one sentence: the generational level of model capability is the starting point for all of the company’s products and commercial logic. From the GLM pre-training architecture to the Wudao series and today’s GLM-5 series, we have focused on one thing for seven years: training stronger models. Every period of rapid revenue growth occurred after model capabilities improved and new task scenarios were unlocked：not before. Capability comes first; business follows. The reversal in revenue mix and the simultaneous growth in volume and pricing in the first half of 2026 have already validated this logic. Going forward, it will continue to be validated by a larger user base, greater commercial scale, and broader global influence. The road ahead is long, but the direction is firm. Thank you.
Q0: How do you view Zhipu’s lead in coding capability, and what is the real long-term moat?
A1: Any single-point lead has a time limit. Ranking first on a coding benchmark may be matched within weeks or months. More important than any one leaderboard position is the ability to iterate continuously. Over approximately the past eleven months, the GLM model family progressed through multiple generations：from 4.6 and 4.7 to 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3. Its capability curve continued to rise, while cost per task remained at a relatively healthy level. The long-term moat is not permanent leadership on every benchmark. It is the ability to maintain faster model iteration, a higher completion rate on real-world tasks, a lower unit cost of intelligence, and continued penetration into higher-value customer workflows.
Q1: Why did you choose coding as the key starting point for breakthroughs in model capability?
A2: Coding is not viewed merely as a product line that can be commercialized quickly. It is a technical bottleneck on the path toward Agents, long-horizon tasks, complex collaborative work, and Fully Self-Training. A complex coding Agent must simultaneously understand requirements, break down tasks, read code, call tools, modify code, run tests, re-plan, and verify results. This systematically trains multi-step planning, error recovery, and self-correction. Whether code runs, whether tests pass, whether performance improves, and whether bugs are fixed can all be objectively verified. Coding therefore provides a scalable, automated, and low-cost feedback environment for reinforcement learning. GLM-5.3’s training environment has expanded from conventional coding exercises to real engineering tasks. Some of these tasks represent an amount of work equivalent to several consecutive days by a senior engineer.
